# Introduction

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/getting-started/introduction.mdx

title: Introduction
description: ShellHub is a centralized SSH gateway for remote access to Linux devices — no VPN, no public IP, no firewall changes

import DiagramReverseConnectivity from '../../components/DiagramReverseConnectivity.astro';

# Introduction

ShellHub is a centralized SSH gateway that gives you remote access to Linux devices over the internet. No public IPs, no VPNs, no firewall changes.

## The problem

Managing SSH access to remote Linux devices is painful. Traditional setups require public IPs, open firewall ports, VPN tunnels, or jump hosts. That works for a handful of servers in a data center — it falls apart when you're dealing with devices behind NAT, CGNAT, or strict corporate firewalls.

If you manage edge devices, IoT gateways, or distributed servers, you've likely dealt with at least one of these:

- Devices behind carrier-grade NAT with no inbound connectivity
- VPN configurations that break when networks change
- Firewall rules that need to be maintained per device
- Jump hosts that become single points of failure
- No visibility into who connected to what, and when

## How ShellHub solves it

ShellHub reverses the connection model. Instead of opening inbound ports on each device, you install a lightweight agent that connects **outbound** to the ShellHub server over HTTPS (port 443). You then access your devices through the ShellHub gateway using a web terminal or your standard SSH client.

<DiagramReverseConnectivity />

The agent initiates the connection from the device side, so it works behind any network topology — NAT, CGNAT, firewalls, proxies. The device never needs a public IP or an open inbound port.

The result:

- **No inbound ports** — Devices connect outbound, so no firewall rules needed
- **No VPN** — Access devices directly through the gateway
- **No public IPs** — Works behind NAT, CGNAT, and corporate firewalls
- **One entry point** — A single URL to reach all your devices
- **Full audit trail** — Every connection is logged with user, device, and timestamp

## What you can do

For details on each feature, see the [Features](/getting-started/features) page.

- **Web terminal** — Open an SSH session from your browser, no client needed
- **Native SSH** — Use OpenSSH, PuTTY, or any SSH client with the device's SSHID
- **SCP and SFTP** — Transfer files to and from devices
- **Public key auth** — Manage SSH keys centrally with per-device and per-user control
- **Firewall rules** — Define who can connect to which devices, from which IPs
- **Session recording** — Record and replay terminal sessions for auditing
- **Device tagging** — Organize devices with labels and filter by tag
- **Multi-tenant** — Isolate devices and teams into namespaces with role-based access
- **Container access** — SSH into Docker containers running on your devices
- **MFA** — Add a second factor to user authentication

## Next steps

- [How it Works](/getting-started/how-it-works) — Understand the core concepts: Server, Agent, Namespace, and SSHID
- [Features](/getting-started/features) — Detailed look at what ShellHub offers
- [Editions](/getting-started/editions) — Compare Community, Cloud, and Enterprise
- [Quick Start](/getting-started/quick-start) — Get ShellHub running and connect your first device

# Quick Start

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/getting-started/quick-start.mdx

title: Quick Start
description: Get ShellHub running and connect your first device in minutes

# Quick Start

This guide gets you from zero to your first SSH session through ShellHub. Pick your path:

- **[ShellHub Cloud](#shellhub-cloud)** — Fastest way. No server setup, start in 2 minutes.
- **[Self-Hosted](#self-hosted)** — Run ShellHub on your own infrastructure with Docker Compose.

Both paths end the same way: installing the agent on a device, accepting it, and connecting via SSH.

## ShellHub Cloud

### 1. Create an account

Go to [cloud.shellhub.io](https://cloud.shellhub.io) and sign up. Verify your email when prompted.

After logging in, you'll be asked to create a **namespace** — this is your workspace that groups your devices, team members, and settings.

Once your namespace is ready, you land on the **dashboard**: an overview of your namespace with device count cards (Accepted, Online, Pending), your Tenant ID, recent sessions, and the left navigation (Dashboard, Devices, Containers, Sessions, Public Keys, Firewall Rules, Secure Vault, Team, Settings).

![ShellHub dashboard](/img/getting-started/dashboard.png)

### 2. Install the agent

In the dashboard, click **Add Device**. You'll get the install script command:

```bash
$ curl -sSf "https://cloud.shellhub.io/install.sh?tenant_id=YOUR_TENANT_ID" | sh
```

Run this on any Linux device you want to manage. The agent installs as a Docker container and connects to ShellHub automatically.

> **Tip:** The agent needs Docker or Podman on the device. For other installation methods (Snap, FreeBSD, Buildroot, Yocto), see [Agent](/agent/overview).

![ShellHub Add Device page showing the installation method chooser and the one-line install command](/img/devices/device-add.gif)

### 3. Accept the device

Open the **Devices** page from the left nav. Your new device appears with **Pending** status, listed with its hostname, SSHID, and operating system. Click **Accept** to approve it — its status moves to **Online** and it's ready to connect.

![ShellHub Devices page on the Pending tab where new devices await acceptance](/img/devices/device-pending.gif)

For everything you can do from here — searching, tagging, renaming, and removing devices — see [Devices](/guides/devices).

### 4. Connect

Click the terminal icon next to the device to open a web SSH session. Enter the device username and password — you're in.

![Device connecting](/img/devices/device-connect.gif)

To connect with your own SSH client:

```bash
$ ssh username@namespace.hostname@cloud.shellhub.io
```

Replace `username` with the device user, `hostname` with the device name shown in the dashboard, and `namespace` with your namespace name.

You should see the device's shell prompt. If you get a connection error, check that the device status shows **Online** in the dashboard.

**Done.** You now have remote SSH access to your device through ShellHub. For web terminal, SSH client, and GUI tool options, see [Connecting to Devices](/guides/connecting).

## Self-Hosted

### Prerequisites

- Docker Engine 20.10+
- Docker Compose v2
- A Linux host with at least 1 GB of RAM
- Ports 80 and 22 available (configurable)

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
$ git clone https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub.git
$ cd shellhub
```

### 2. Generate keys

ShellHub uses cryptographic keys for device authentication:

```bash
$ make keygen
```

### 3. Start the services

```bash
$ make start
```

First run pulls container images and takes a few minutes. Once done, all services are running.

### 4. Create your account

Run the setup script to generate a setup URL:

```bash
$ ./bin/setup
```

Open the generated URL in your browser. Create your admin account and choose a namespace name.

### 5. Install the agent

In the dashboard, click **Add Device** and copy the install command:

```bash
$ curl -sSf "http://YOUR_SERVER/install.sh?tenant_id=YOUR_TENANT_ID" | sh
```

Run this on the Linux device you want to manage. Replace `YOUR_SERVER` with your ShellHub server's address.

### 6. Accept the device

The device appears with **Pending** status in the dashboard. Click **Accept**.

### 7. Connect

Click the terminal icon to open a web session, or use your SSH client:

```bash
$ ssh username@namespace.hostname@your-server.com
```

You should see the device's shell prompt. If you get a connection error, check that the device status shows **Online** in the dashboard.

**Done.** Your self-hosted ShellHub instance is running and your first device is connected.

### Configuration

Customize the deployment with a `.env.override` file in the project root:

```bash
SHELLHUB_HTTP_PORT=8080
SHELLHUB_SSH_PORT=2222
SHELLHUB_DOMAIN=shellhub.example.com
SHELLHUB_AUTO_SSL=true
```

See [Configuring](/self-hosted/configuring) for the full reference.

### Stopping

```bash
$ make stop
```

Data persists in Docker volumes. Your devices and configuration survive restarts.

## Next steps

- [Agent](/agent/overview) — Install the agent on Docker, Snap, FreeBSD, or WSL
- [Embedded Linux](/embedded-linux/overview) — Embed the agent into Buildroot or Yocto images
- [FAQ](/getting-started/faq) — Common questions and answers
- [Connecting to Devices](/guides/connecting) — Web terminal, SSH client, and GUI tools
- [Self-Hosted Deployment](/self-hosted/deploying) — Production deployment guide

# Connecting via SSH

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/connecting.mdx

title: Connecting via SSH
description: Access devices using the web terminal or native SSH clients

# Connecting via SSH

ShellHub gives you two ways to reach your devices: a web terminal in the dashboard and native SSH client support.

## Web terminal

From the **Devices** page, click the terminal icon next to any online device. A browser-based terminal opens with full shell access — no software to install on your workstation.

Supports copy/paste, terminal resizing, and multiple simultaneous tabs.

![Device connecting](/img/devices/device-connect.gif)

## Native SSH

Connect with any standard SSH client (anything supporting SSH 2.0 or later) using the device's SSHID — a virtual address that routes your connection through ShellHub to the right device.

> **New to SSHID?** It's ShellHub's virtual addressing system for SSH. [See how it works →](/getting-started/how-it-works#sshid--virtual-hosting-for-ssh)

### Find the SSHID

Open the device from the [Devices](/guides/devices) page. Its SSHID is shown at the top of the device details page, with a copy button next to it.

![Device details page showing the SSHID with a copy button](/img/devices/device-details.png)

### SSHID format

```
<namespace>.<device-name>@<server>
```

To connect, prefix the SSHID with the operating-system user you want to log in as:

```
<username>@<namespace>.<device-name>@<server>
```

### OpenSSH

```bash
$ ssh root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

If your server uses a non-default SSH port:

```bash
$ ssh -p 2222 root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

### SSH config

Add devices to `~/.ssh/config` for quicker access:

```
Host web-server
    HostName shellhub.example.com
    User root@myteam.web-server
    Port 22
```

Then:

```bash
$ ssh web-server
```

## Authentication

**Password** — Enter the device's local user password when prompted. Works for any user account on the device.

**Public key** — If you've uploaded your SSH key to ShellHub, authentication happens without a password. See [Public Keys](/guides/public-keys).

## Next steps

- [File Transfer](/guides/file-transfer) — SCP, SFTP, and rsync through ShellHub
- [Port Forwarding](/guides/port-forwarding) — SSH tunnels to access remote services locally

## Troubleshooting

**Connection refused** — Check that the device is online in the dashboard and the SSH port matches your server config.

**Permission denied** — Verify the username and password. For public keys, check the key is uploaded and its filters allow access to this device.

**Timeout** — Make sure the ShellHub server is reachable and the SSH port isn't blocked on the client side.

---

# Container Access

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/container-access.mdx

title: Container Access
description: SSH into Docker containers running on your devices through ShellHub

# Container Access

ShellHub lets you SSH directly into Docker containers running on a host. The **ShellHub Connector** runs on the Docker host, connects to the Docker API, and exposes the running containers as accessible targets — you connect to a container the same way you connect to a [device](/guides/devices).

## How it works

The ShellHub Connector is the component that makes containers reachable. Installed on the Docker host, it talks to the Docker API, detects running containers, and registers each one in ShellHub. Every container gets its own SSHID, so you can connect to it directly through the ShellHub gateway.

The connection path:

```
You → ShellHub Gateway → Connector (on host) → Docker exec → Container shell
```

No SSH server needs to run inside the container. The Connector bridges the SSH session and the container's shell.

## Registering a Docker host

To add Docker containers to ShellHub, install the ShellHub Connector on the Docker host. Open the **Containers** page and click **Add Container** to open the *Registering a Docker Host* drawer.

![ShellHub Containers page with the Registering a Docker Host drawer open, showing the one-line Connector install command](/img/containers/add-docker-host.png)

The easiest way is the one-line install script. It installs and starts the Connector, which connects to the Docker API and exposes the running containers within ShellHub:

```bash
$ curl -sSf <server>/install.sh | TENANT_ID=<tenant> SERVER_ADDRESS=<server> sh -s connector
```

The `connector` argument tells the [install script](/agent/install-script) to set up the Connector rather than a regular device agent. Substitute your server address and namespace tenant ID, both shown in the drawer.

Once the Connector is running, any Docker containers on the host automatically appear under the **Pending** tab on the Containers page. Accept a container to allow SSH access to it — the Containers page lists containers across **Accepted**, **Pending**, and **Rejected** tabs, the same acceptance flow used for [devices](/guides/devices).

## Connecting to a container

Once accepted, use the container's SSHID just like a regular device:

```bash
$ ssh root@myteam.my-container@shellhub.example.com
```

From the web dashboard, accepted containers appear on the **Containers** page with a terminal icon for web-based access.

## Container visibility

The Connector lists containers that are:

- **Running** — Stopped or paused containers are not shown
- **On the same Docker host** — The Connector only sees containers on the machine where it's installed

When a container starts or stops, the Connector updates ShellHub automatically.

## Use cases

**Debug a running service** — Drop into a production container to inspect logs, check config files, or run diagnostic commands without redeploying.

**Access isolated environments** — Reach containers that have no exposed ports and no SSH server installed.

**Audit container access** — All container SSH sessions are logged the same way as device sessions, with full audit trail and optional [session recording](/guides/session-recording).

## Limitations

- The ShellHub Connector must run on the Docker host, not inside the container
- Container access requires Docker to be installed and the Docker API accessible to the Connector
- If a container is recreated (new container ID), it appears as a new entry

---

# Device Management

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/devices.mdx

title: Device Management
description: Monitor and manage your fleet of Linux devices

# Device Management

Devices are Linux machines running the ShellHub agent. Once connected, you can monitor their status, organize them with tags, and open SSH sessions from anywhere.

![ShellHub Devices page listing accepted devices](/img/devices/device-list.png)

## Adding a device

Click **Add Device** on the Devices page and choose an installation method — **Auto Detect** (recommended), **Docker**, or **Standalone**. ShellHub generates a one-line install command that already carries your namespace's **Tenant ID** and the **server address**, so all you have to do is run it on the target machine.

![ShellHub Add Device page showing the installation method chooser and the one-line install command](/img/devices/device-add.gif)

Once the agent starts, the device registers and appears in the **Pending** tab. You must accept it before anyone can connect — see [Accepting and rejecting](#accepting-and-rejecting) below.

For other installation methods, see the [Agent Overview](/agent/overview). For details on what the generated command does, see the [Install Script](/agent/install-script).

## Lifecycle

Every device goes through a simple lifecycle:

1. **Pending** — The agent registered with ShellHub, but the device hasn't been approved yet
2. **Accepted** — Approved and ready for SSH connections
3. **Rejected** — Explicitly denied access

New devices always start as pending. You must manually accept them before anyone can connect. This prevents unauthorized devices from joining your namespace.

## Device information

Each device reports the following through the agent:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Name** | Hostname (editable) |
| **SSHID** | Unique identifier for SSH connections |
| **MAC address** | Network interface identifier |
| **OS** | Operating system and version |
| **Architecture** | CPU arch (amd64, arm64, armv7, etc.) |
| **Last seen** | Last heartbeat timestamp |
| **Status** | Online or offline |

## SSHID

Every accepted device gets a unique SSH identifier:

```
<username>@<namespace>.<device-name>.<server>
```

For example:

```bash
$ ssh root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

This works with any standard SSH client. See [Connecting via SSH](/guides/connecting) for details.

## Accepting and rejecting

From the **Devices** page:

- **Pending** tab — Accept or reject new devices
- **Accepted** tab — View active devices, remove access if needed
- **Rejected** tab — Re-accept previously rejected devices

![ShellHub Devices page on the Pending tab where new devices await acceptance](/img/devices/device-pending.gif)

## Renaming

You can rename a device from the device details page without affecting the underlying hostname. Names must be unique within a namespace and can contain lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.

## Removing

Removing a device reverts it to pending. The agent keeps running on the device, but it can't receive connections until re-accepted. To fully disconnect, uninstall the agent from the device.

## Next steps

- [Agent Overview](/agent/overview) — Deploy the agent
- [Tags](/guides/tags) — Organize devices
- [Connecting via SSH](/guides/connecting) — Access your devices

---

# File Transfer

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/file-transfer.mdx

title: File Transfer
description: Transfer files to and from devices using SCP and SFTP through ShellHub

# File Transfer

Move files between your workstation and remote devices using standard SCP and SFTP commands. ShellHub routes file transfers through the same gateway as SSH sessions — no extra ports or configuration needed.

## SCP

Copy files using the device's SSHID, the same address you use for SSH.

### Upload a file

```bash
$ scp file.txt root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/tmp/
```

### Download a file

```bash
$ scp root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/var/log/app.log ./
```

### Transfer a directory

Use `-r` for recursive transfers:

```bash
$ scp -r ./deploy root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/opt/app/
```

### Non-default SSH port

If your ShellHub server listens on a different port, use `-P` (uppercase):

```bash
$ scp -P 2222 file.txt root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/tmp/
```

## SFTP

SFTP provides an interactive file browser with the same SSHID:

```bash
$ sftp root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
sftp> ls /var/log
sftp> get /var/log/syslog ./syslog.local
sftp> put config.yaml /etc/app/config.yaml
sftp> exit
```

### Common SFTP commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `ls` | List remote files |
| `cd` | Change remote directory |
| `get <file>` | Download file |
| `put <file>` | Upload file |
| `mkdir <dir>` | Create remote directory |
| `rm <file>` | Delete remote file |

## rsync

rsync works over SSH, so it works through ShellHub:

```bash
$ rsync -avz ./project/ root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/opt/project/
```

For non-default ports:

```bash
$ rsync -avz -e "ssh -p 2222" ./project/ root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com:/opt/project/
```

## GUI clients

Any SFTP client that supports standard SSH connections works with ShellHub. Set the host to your ShellHub server (`shellhub.example.com`), the port to your SSH port, and set the username to `<username>@<namespace>.<device>` (for example, `root@myteam.web-server`).

Popular clients: FileZilla, WinSCP, Cyberduck, Transmit.

## Troubleshooting

**Permission denied** — Check that the SSH user has write access to the target directory on the device.

**Connection timeout during large transfers** — The transfer goes through the ShellHub tunnel. For very large files, consider compressing before transfer or using rsync with `--partial` for resumable transfers.

**Port mismatch** — SCP uses `-P` (uppercase) for port, while SSH uses `-p` (lowercase). SFTP uses `-P` as well.

---

# Firewall Rules

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/firewall-rules.mdx

title: Firewall Rules
description: Control SSH connections to your devices with fine-grained allow and deny rules

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Firewall Rules

<EditionBanner />

Define rules that allow or deny SSH connections based on source IP, username, and target device. Rules are evaluated before the connection reaches the device.

![The Firewall Rules page showing a table of rules with Priority, Action, Source IP, Username, Device Filter, and Status columns](/img/firewall/firewall-rules.png)

## How it works

When an SSH connection comes in, ShellHub evaluates your firewall rules before granting access:

1. Rules are sorted by priority (highest number first)
2. Each active rule checks the connection against its conditions — source IP, username, and device filter
3. The first matching rule wins, and its action (allow or deny) is applied
4. If no rule matches, the connection proceeds normally

This gives you centralized network-level access control without touching individual device configurations.

## Creating a rule

1. Go to **Firewall Rules** in the sidebar
2. Click **Add Rule**
3. Set the rule's priority, policy, and status
4. Configure source IP, username, and device filters
5. Save

![The New Firewall Rule drawer with Status, Priority, Policy, Source IP, Username, and Device filter fields](/img/firewall/add-rule.png)

The rule takes effect immediately for new connections.

## Rule fields

### Status

Toggle a rule **Active** or **Inactive**. Inactive rules are skipped during evaluation, letting you disable a rule temporarily without deleting it.

### Priority

An integer that determines evaluation order. Higher values are evaluated first. Priority cannot be 0.

If two rules could match the same connection, the one with the higher priority wins. Use this to layer broad defaults with specific overrides.

### Policy

The action to take when the rule matches:

- **Allow** — Permit the connection
- **Deny** — Block the connection

### Source IP

Which client IPs the rule applies to:

- **All devices** — Matches any source IP
- **Restrict with regexp** — A Go-compatible regex tested against the client's IP address

### Username

Which SSH usernames the rule applies to:

- **All users** — Matches any username
- **Restrict with regexp** — A Go-compatible regex tested against the username in the SSH connection

### Device filter

Which devices the rule applies to. Choose one:

- **All devices** — Matches every device (hostname pattern `.*`)
- **Restrict by hostname regexp** — A regex tested against the device hostname
- **Restrict by tags** — Up to 3 tags. The rule applies to devices that have those tags.

## Matching patterns

Filters use Go regex syntax. Common patterns:

| Pattern | Matches | Use case |
|---------|---------|----------|
| `.*` | Everything | Wildcard, match all |
| `root` | Exactly `root` | Single username |
| `192\.168\.1\..*` | `192.168.1.0/24` range | Local subnet |
| `10\.0\..*` | Any IP starting with `10.0.` | VPN range |
| `web-.*` | `web-01`, `web-prod`, etc. | Hostname prefix |
| `.*-staging` | `app-staging`, `db-staging` | Hostname suffix |

Note: Dots in IP addresses must be escaped with `\` since `.` matches any character in regex.

## Examples

| Priority | Policy | Source IP | Username | Device filter | Effect |
|----------|--------|-----------|----------|---------------|--------|
| 100 | Deny | `.*` | `root` | Hostname: `.*` | Block root access from everywhere |
| 200 | Allow | `192\.168\.1\..*` | `root` | Hostname: `.*` | Allow root from local network (overrides rule above) |
| 50 | Deny | `.*` | `.*` | Tags: `production` | Block all access to production devices |
| 150 | Allow | `10\.0\.0\..*` | `deploy` | Tags: `production` | Allow deploy user from VPN to production |
| 10 | Deny | `.*` | `guest` | Hostname: `.*` | Block guest user everywhere |

**How these rules interact:**

- `deploy` user at `10.0.0.5` → production device: Rule 200 doesn't match (wrong username), rule 150 matches → **allowed**
- `root` at `192.168.1.10` → any device: Rule 200 matches → **allowed** (never reaches rule 100's deny)
- `root` at `203.0.113.50` → any device: Rule 200 doesn't match (wrong IP), rule 100 matches → **denied**
- `guest` from anywhere → any device: Rule 10 matches → **denied**

## Managing rules

From the **Firewall Rules** page, you can edit any field of a rule or delete it. Changes take effect immediately for new connections. Active connections are not affected by rule changes.

## Best practices

- **Start with deny rules at low priority** — Set broad deny policies as a baseline, then add targeted allow rules at higher priorities
- **Use tags for group-based rules** — Easier to maintain than hostname patterns as your fleet changes
- **Escape dots in IP patterns** — Write `192\.168\.1\..*` not `192.168.1..*` to avoid matching unintended IPs
- **Keep priorities spaced out** — Use increments of 10 or 100 so you can insert rules later without renumbering
- **Disable before deleting** — Toggle a rule inactive first to verify the change before removing it permanently
- **Document your rules** — Use consistent priority ranges (e.g., 1-99 for defaults, 100-199 for team rules, 200+ for exceptions)

---

# Local Authentication

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/local-authentication.mdx

title: Local Authentication
description: Manage built-in username and password sign-in for your ShellHub instance

# Local Authentication

Local authentication is ShellHub's built-in sign-in method: users authenticate with an email and password stored securely in ShellHub's own database, with no external identity provider required. It is enabled by default, so users can register and sign in immediately after installation.

## Enabling and disabling

An instance **admin** controls local authentication from the **Admin Console** under **Settings → Authentication**, using the **Local Authentication** toggle.

![The Admin Console Authentication page with the Local Authentication and SAML Authentication toggles](/img/auth/admin-authentication.png)

When local authentication is **disabled**, the email-and-password login is turned off and users sign in through [SSO](/guides/sso) instead.

At least one authentication method must remain enabled at all times. Before disabling local login, make sure an alternative such as SAML is configured and tested.

## Enabling local login for a specific user

You can grant a single user the ability to sign in with a password — useful, for example, for an SSO-provisioned account that needs a fallback login. This preserves the user's existing authentication methods and adds local login as an option.

1. Go to **Users** in the Admin Console
2. Find the target user and select **Enable Local Authentication**
3. Confirm the action
4. ShellHub generates a temporary password — securely share it with the user

The user should change the temporary password after their first successful login.

## Next steps

- [Single Sign-On (SAML)](/guides/sso) — Sign in through an external identity provider
- [Multi-Factor Authentication](/guides/mfa) — Add TOTP-based 2FA to accounts
- [Administration](/self-hosted/administration) — Manage your ShellHub instance

---

# Multi-Factor Authentication

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/mfa.mdx

title: Multi-Factor Authentication
description: Protect your ShellHub account with TOTP-based two-factor authentication

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Multi-Factor Authentication

<EditionBanner />

Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) adds a second verification step to your account login. With MFA enabled, you provide a time-based one-time password (TOTP) from an authenticator app in addition to your password. It is configured per user account and works with any TOTP app, such as Google Authenticator, 1Password, or Authy.

## How it works

When MFA is active, every login requires two factors:

1. Your password
2. A 6-digit TOTP code from your authenticator app

If you lose access to your authenticator, you can regain entry using a one-time recovery code or your recovery email.

## Enabling MFA

Open your **Profile** page and find the **Security** section, then click **Enable MFA**.

![The Profile page Security section with the Enable MFA option](/img/account/mfa-enable.gif)

The setup runs in three steps.

### Step 1 — Set a recovery email

Provide a recovery email address. This is required and is used to regain access if you ever lose both your authenticator app and your recovery codes.

![Recovery mail](/img/account/mfa-recovery-mail.png)

### Step 2 - Save 

Download or copy the recovery codes, check "I have saved my recovery codes in a secure location" and then click "Next Step".

![Recovery codes screen](/img/account/mfa-recovery-codes.png)

### Step 3 — Scan the QR code

Open your authenticator app and scan the displayed TOTP QR code (or enter the secret manually). Enter the 6-digit code your app generates to confirm, then complete the setup.

![MFA QR Code waiting to be scanned](/img/account/mfa-setup.png)

## Logging in with MFA

After enabling MFA, the login flow gains a second step:

1. Enter your email and password as usual
2. When prompted, enter the current 6-digit code from your authenticator app
3. Submit to complete the login

![Login requiring 6-digit code](/img/account/mfa-login.png)

## Account recovery

If you lose access to your authenticator app, you can still get back into your account.

| You have | How to recover |
|----------|----------------|
| A recovery code | Choose to use a recovery code at the MFA prompt and enter one of your saved codes. Each code works only once. |
| Only your recovery email | Request recovery via your recovery email. ShellHub sends a code that lets you disable MFA and regain access. |

On Enterprise instances, self-service recovery by email may be unavailable — contact your instance administrator to reset MFA on your account.

## Next steps

- [Local Authentication](/guides/local-authentication) — Built-in username and password sign-in
- [Single Sign-On (SAML)](/guides/sso) — Sign in through an external identity provider
- [Settings](/guides/settings) — Manage your account and namespace

---

# Namespaces

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/namespaces.mdx

title: Namespaces
description: Isolated workspaces that contain your devices, sessions, keys, and team

# Namespaces

A namespace is an isolated workspace. Each one has its own devices, SSH keys, firewall rules, sessions, and team members. Everything in ShellHub lives inside a namespace.

Use namespaces to separate environments, projects, teams, or customers on a single ShellHub server.

## Creating a namespace

Your first namespace is created when you set up ShellHub. To create additional namespaces:

1. Click the namespace selector in the dashboard header
2. Select **Create Namespace**
3. Pick a name — lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens

> Pick a short name. It becomes part of every device's SSH address.

![Switching namespaces](/img/settings/namespace-create.gif)

## Switching namespaces

Click the namespace selector in the top bar to see every namespace you belong to. Select one to switch — the dashboard, devices, sessions, and all other pages update to show that namespace's data. Your active namespace is always shown in the selector, so you can confirm which one you're working in at a glance.

![Switching namespaces](/img/settings/namespace-switch.gif)

## What's inside a namespace

| Resource | Scoped to namespace? |
|----------|---------------------|
| Devices | Yes — each device belongs to one namespace |
| Sessions | Yes — session history is per namespace |
| Public keys | Yes — keys are scoped to the namespace |
| Firewall rules | Yes — rules apply within the namespace |
| Tags | Yes — tags exist within a namespace |
| Web endpoints | Yes — endpoints are per namespace |
| Team members | Yes — members and roles are per namespace |
| Settings | Yes — recording, announcements, MFA are per namespace |

A user can be a member of multiple namespaces with different roles in each — see [Team](/guides/team) to manage members and roles.

## Finding your Tenant ID

Every namespace has a unique **Tenant ID**. This is how ShellHub identifies a namespace — agents use it to connect their devices to the right namespace, and it's the identifier you use when integrating with the ShellHub API.

To find it, open **Settings** and look at the **General** section. The Tenant ID is listed there with a copy button.

![Namespace Settings page showing the Tenant ID being copied](/img/settings/namespace-copy-tenant-id.gif)

Make sure you're in the correct namespace before copying — switch with the namespace selector if you manage more than one. See [Settings](/guides/settings) for the rest of the namespace configuration.

## Namespace in SSHIDs

The namespace is part of every device's SSHID:

```
<username>@<namespace>.<device-name>.<server>
```

For example:

```bash
$ ssh root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

Here `myteam` is the namespace. Your team will type it in every SSH command, so keep it short and descriptive.

## Deleting a namespace

Only the owner can delete a namespace. This permanently removes all devices, keys, firewall rules, session history, and member access. The action is irreversible.

![Deleting namespaces](/img/settings/namespace-delete.gif)

## Next steps

- [Team](/guides/team) — Manage members, roles, and API keys
- [Settings](/guides/settings) — Configure session recording, announcements, and MFA

---

# Port Forwarding

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/port-forwarding.mdx

title: Port Forwarding
description: Access remote services through SSH tunnels via ShellHub

# Port Forwarding

SSH port forwarding lets you access services running on remote devices as if they were local. ShellHub supports standard SSH tunneling — local forwarding, remote forwarding, and SOCKS proxies all work through the gateway.

## Local port forwarding

Forward a port from a remote device to your local machine. This is the most common use case: accessing a database, web app, or admin panel that's only listening on the device's localhost.

```bash
$ ssh -L <local-port>:localhost:<remote-port> <sshid>
```

### Access a remote database

Forward PostgreSQL from a device to your workstation:

```bash
$ ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 root@myteam.db-server@shellhub.example.com
```

Now connect your database client to `localhost:5432` — traffic flows through the ShellHub tunnel to the device.

### Access a web admin panel

Forward a web interface running on port 8080:

```bash
$ ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 root@myteam.monitoring@shellhub.example.com
```

Open `http://localhost:8080` in your browser.

### Forward to a different host

The device can forward to other hosts on its local network:

```bash
$ ssh -L 3306:192.168.1.50:3306 root@myteam.gateway@shellhub.example.com
```

This reaches a MySQL server at `192.168.1.50` through the ShellHub-connected device.

## Remote port forwarding

Expose a local service through the remote device:

```bash
$ ssh -R <remote-port>:localhost:<local-port> <sshid>
```

Example — make your local dev server available on the device:

```bash
$ ssh -R 3000:localhost:3000 root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

## Dynamic port forwarding (SOCKS proxy)

Create a SOCKS proxy that routes all traffic through the remote device:

```bash
$ ssh -D 1080 root@myteam.web-server@shellhub.example.com
```

Configure your browser or application to use `localhost:1080` as a SOCKS5 proxy. All traffic exits from the device's network — useful for accessing internal services or testing from the device's network perspective.

## Multiple tunnels

Combine multiple `-L` flags in one command:

```bash
$ ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 -L 6379:localhost:6379 -L 8080:localhost:8080 root@myteam.app-server@shellhub.example.com
```

## SSH config

Add forwarding rules to `~/.ssh/config` for convenience:

```
Host myteam-db
    HostName shellhub.example.com
    User root@myteam.db-server
    LocalForward 5432 localhost:5432
    LocalForward 6379 localhost:6379
```

Then just:

```bash
$ ssh myteam-db
```

## Background tunnels

Run a tunnel in the background without opening an interactive shell:

```bash
$ ssh -fNL 5432:localhost:5432 root@myteam.db-server@shellhub.example.com
```

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `-f` | Go to background after authentication |
| `-N` | Don't execute a remote command |
| `-L` | Local port forwarding |

## Troubleshooting

**Address already in use** — Another process is using the local port. Pick a different local port: `-L 15432:localhost:5432`.

**Channel open failed** — The target service isn't running on the device, or it's not listening on the expected port. SSH into the device and verify with `ss -tlnp`.

**Connection drops after idle** — Add keepalive to your SSH config:

```
Host *
    ServerAliveInterval 60
    ServerAliveCountMax 3
```

---

# Public Keys

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/public-keys.mdx

title: Public Keys
description: Manage SSH keys centrally with fine-grained access control

# Public Keys

Upload your SSH public key once to ShellHub and use it to authenticate across all your devices. No need to copy keys to each machine. Key-based authentication is passwordless and more secure than passwords, which are vulnerable to brute-force login attempts.

![The Public Keys page listing registered SSH keys with their scope, fingerprint, and management actions](/img/public-keys/public-keys.png)

The **Public Keys** page lists every key registered in your namespace along with its scope, fingerprint, and the date it was added. From here you can add a new key, edit an existing one, or remove it.

## How it works

Traditional SSH key management requires placing your public key in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on every device. With ShellHub, keys are stored on the server and checked during connection:

1. You upload your public key to ShellHub
2. When you [connect via SSH](/guides/connecting), the server checks your key against the stored keys
3. If a match is found and the filters allow access, authentication succeeds

No keys are copied to the devices themselves.

## Adding a key

1. Go to **Public Keys** in the sidebar
2. Click **Add Key**
3. Paste your public key (contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` or similar)
4. Give it a descriptive name
5. Configure access filters
6. Save

Supported types: Ed25519 (recommended), RSA, ECDSA.

## Access filters

Each key has two filters that control where it works:

### Username filter

Which device username the key can authenticate as:

- **All users** (`.*`) — Works for any username
- **Specific user** (e.g., `root`) — Only works when connecting as that user

### Device filter

Which devices the key can access. Choose one:

- **Hostname pattern** — A regex matching device names (e.g., `web-.*` matches `web-01`, `web-02`)
- **Tags** — One or more tags. The key only works on devices with those tags.

### Examples

| Key name | Username | Device filter | Effect |
|----------|----------|---------------|--------|
| Deploy key | `deploy` | Tags: `production` | `deploy` user on production devices only |
| Admin key | `.*` | Hostname: `.*` | Full access everywhere |
| Web team | `root` | Tags: `web` | Root on web-tagged devices only |

## Managing keys

From the **Public Keys** page, you can edit a key's name and filters or delete it. Deleting a key takes effect immediately — the next connection attempt with that key is denied.

## Generating a key pair

```bash
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-email@example.com"
```

This creates `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (private, keep secret) and `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` (public, upload to ShellHub).

## Best practices

- **Use Ed25519 keys** — Smaller, faster, more secure than RSA
- **One key per person** — Simplifies revocation
- **Use tag-based filters** — Easier to maintain as your fleet grows
- **Name keys descriptively** — Include owner and purpose (e.g., "alice-deploy")

---

# Session Recording

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/session-recording.mdx

title: Session Recording
description: Record and replay SSH sessions for auditing and compliance

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Session Recording

<EditionBanner />

ShellHub can record all terminal I/O during SSH sessions. Every keystroke, command output, and timing is captured — then you can replay sessions in the dashboard exactly as they happened.

## Enabling recording

Session recording is configured per namespace:

1. Go to [**Settings**](/guides/settings) in the dashboard
2. Toggle **Session Recording** on
3. All new SSH sessions in this namespace will be recorded

Existing sessions are not affected. Recording starts from the moment you enable it.

![Session recording playback](/img/sessions/session-recording-enable.gif)

## Viewing recordings

Recorded sessions are marked on the [**Sessions**](/guides/sessions) page. Open the session's detail page and click **Play Recording** to launch the player.

The player replays terminal output in real time — you see exactly what the user saw, including:

- Commands typed
- Command output and responses
- Timing between keystrokes
- Terminal resizing

![Session recording playback](/img/sessions/session-play.gif)

Use the playback controls at the bottom to pause and resume, scrub through the timeline (elapsed and total time are shown alongside the scrubber), and adjust playback speed.

## What gets recorded

| Recorded | Not recorded |
|----------|-------------|
| All terminal output (stdout/stderr) | File transfer content (SCP/SFTP payloads) |
| Commands typed (stdin) | Port forwarding traffic |
| Terminal resize events | |
| Session start/end timestamps | |

## Use cases

### Security audit

Review commands executed on sensitive systems. If an incident occurs, you have a complete record of what happened during every session.

### Compliance

Maintain access records for regulatory requirements like SOC 2, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS. Session recordings provide evidence that access was authorized and appropriate.

### Training

Record standard operating procedures and share the recordings with team members. New engineers can see exactly how experienced operators handle common tasks.

### Incident response

When something goes wrong, replay the session to understand the sequence of events. No more guessing what commands were run or relying on shell history.

## Storage

Recordings are stored on the ShellHub server. Storage usage depends on session activity — text-based terminal sessions are compact, but long or high-output sessions (e.g., compiling, streaming logs) generate more data.

For self-hosted deployments, monitor your storage usage and consider retention policies for old recordings.

## Privacy considerations

Session recording captures everything displayed in the terminal. This may include sensitive data like passwords typed in interactive prompts, environment variables, or file contents viewed with `cat`.

Make sure your team knows recording is enabled. Consider:

- Enabling recording only for namespaces that require it
- Using [connection announcements](/guides/settings#connection-announcement) to notify users
- Defining data retention policies that align with your compliance requirements

---

# Sessions

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/sessions.mdx

title: Sessions
description: Monitor and audit SSH sessions

# Sessions

Every SSH connection through ShellHub is recorded as a session and stored on the server for auditing. You get visibility into who connected to which device, when, and for how long — without instrumenting anything on the devices themselves.

![The Sessions page listing active and historical SSH sessions](/img/sessions/session-list.png)

## Viewing sessions

The **Sessions** page lists all sessions in the current namespace:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Device** | Target device name |
| **Username** | Linux user used to authenticate |
| **IP address** | Client's source IP |
| **Started** | Session start time |
| **Last seen** | Last activity timestamp |
| **Status** | Active or closed |

## Active vs. closed

- **Active** — Connection is open, user is connected
- **Closed** — Session ended (user disconnected or connection dropped)

## Session details

Select any session to open its detail view. For audit purposes, ShellHub records metadata about the connection — the target device, the authenticating user, the client's source IP, whether authentication succeeded, and a timeline of activity from connection through close.

![A session detail page showing the session flow timeline, details, device, and play recording button](/img/sessions/session-detail.png)

The **Session flow** timeline walks through the session step by step — connection established from an IP, authenticated as a user, pseudo-terminal opened, commands executed, session recorded, and session closed. The **Details** panel shows the session UID, source IP, and start/end times, while the **Device** panel identifies the target. If the session was recorded, use **Play Recording** to replay it.

## Session recording

Sessions can be recorded for auditing and compliance. When enabled, ShellHub captures all terminal I/O and lets you replay sessions in the dashboard.

See [Session Recording](/guides/session-recording) for setup and details.

---

# Settings

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/settings.mdx

title: Settings
description: Configure namespace settings — session recording, connection announcements, and more

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Settings

Namespace settings control behavior that applies to all devices and sessions within the namespace. Only the Owner and Administrators can modify settings.

![Namespace Settings page](/img/settings/namespace-settings.png)

## General

The **General** section identifies the namespace:

- **Name** — the namespace display name. It also forms part of the SSHID used to connect (`<username>@<namespace>.<hostname>`).
- **Type** — whether the namespace is a **team** or **user** namespace.
- **Tenant ID** — the unique identifier for the namespace, with a copy button. Use this identifier when integrating with the [ShellHub API](/developers/api-reference) or registering agents. See [Namespaces](/guides/namespaces) for how the Tenant ID ties devices and members together.

## Session recording

<EditionBanner />

The **SSH** section controls behavior for SSH connections to the namespace.

When enabled, ShellHub records all terminal I/O during SSH sessions. Recordings can be replayed in the dashboard for auditing, compliance, and troubleshooting.

Toggle **Session Recording** On to start capturing new sessions. Existing sessions are not affected.

See [Session Recording](/guides/session-recording) for details on playback, storage, and privacy considerations.

## Connection announcement

The **SSH Banner** is a message shown to users when they connect via SSH. Use it to notify about maintenance windows, acceptable use policies, or recording notices.

The banner supports multiple lines, and the settings page shows a preview of how it will appear. When set, users see the banner text before their SSH session starts.

## MFA requirement

<EditionBanner />

When enabled, all namespace members must have multi-factor authentication configured on their account. Members without MFA will be prompted to set it up before they can access the namespace.

## Device limits

View the maximum number of devices allowed in this namespace based on your plan. The dashboard shows current usage against the limit.

| Edition | Default limit |
|---------|--------------|
| Community | 3 devices |
| Cloud | Based on subscription |
| Enterprise | Unlimited |

# Single Sign-On (SAML)

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/sso.mdx

title: Single Sign-On (SAML)
description: Let users sign in to ShellHub through an external SAML identity provider

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Single Sign-On (SAML)

<EditionBanner />

SAML Single Sign-On lets users authenticate through an external identity provider (IdP) instead of registering credentials directly in ShellHub. ShellHub acts as the service provider (SP), trusting your IdP to verify identities. One IdP can be active at a time per instance.

SSO is configured by an instance **admin** in the **Admin Console**. Once enabled, users see a **Login with SSO** button on the login page.

## Enabling SAML

In the **Admin Console**, go to **Settings → Authentication** and toggle **SAML Authentication** on, then configure your IdP.

![The Admin Console Authentication page with the Local Authentication and SAML Authentication toggles](/img/auth/admin-authentication.png)

You can configure the IdP in one of two ways:

| Method | When to use |
|--------|-------------|
| **Metadata URL** | Your IdP publishes a metadata URL. Enable *Use IdP Metadata URL* and paste it — ShellHub imports the configuration automatically. |
| **Manual entry** | Enter the IdP's sign-in URL, entity ID, and X.509 certificate directly in the form. |

After saving, configure your IdP to allow callbacks to ShellHub's authentication endpoint:

```
https://<your-instance>/api/user/saml/auth
```

## Attribute mapping

ShellHub identifies users from attributes in the SAML assertion. Two attributes are required:

- **Email** — the primary identifier for the user (default attribute: `emailaddress`)
- **Display name** — shown throughout the interface (default attribute: `displayname`)

If your IdP uses different attribute names, override them under **Advanced Settings → SAML Mappings**. Mapping is case-insensitive. Authentication fails if a required attribute is missing from the assertion.

## Signed AuthnRequests (optional)

For added security, you can sign the SAML authentication requests ShellHub sends to your IdP. Enable **Sign authorization requests** under **Advanced Settings**: ShellHub generates an X.509 certificate (valid for one year) and signs every request with it. Download the SP certificate and register it with your IdP so it can verify request authenticity.

The certificate is regenerated when you disable and re-enable SAML or change the configuration while signing is enabled — update your IdP with the new certificate afterward.

## How SSO login works

When a user clicks **Login with SSO**, ShellHub handles the assertion based on whether the account already exists:

- **First-time users** — ShellHub creates the account automatically, importing the email and name from the assertion. These accounts have no password and rely on the IdP.
- **Existing users** — ShellHub matches the assertion email to the existing account and enables SAML for it, preserving any existing login methods (a user with a password can still sign in either way).

Switching to a new IdP migrates existing SAML users automatically, with no action required from them.

## Next steps

- [Local Authentication](/guides/local-authentication) — Built-in username and password sign-in
- [Multi-Factor Authentication](/guides/mfa) — Add TOTP-based 2FA to accounts
- [Administration](/self-hosted/administration) — Manage your ShellHub instance

---

# Tags

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/tags.mdx

title: Tags
description: Organize and filter devices with tags

# Tags

Tags are labels you assign to devices to organize your fleet. Use them to group by environment, location, role, or anything that fits your workflow.

## Assigning tags

On the **Devices** page, open a device's **Actions** menu and click **Edit tags**. Enter tags separated by commas or spaces (for example, `production, web`), then save. Each device supports up to 3 tags, and tag names can contain lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.

## Filtering

On the **Devices** page, use the **Tags** menu to filter the list by one or more tags. Combine tags for more specific views.

## Managing tags globally

Manage every tag in your namespace from one place: go to **Settings → Tags**, where you can rename or remove any tag across all devices.

## Tags + access control

Tags drive two of ShellHub's access-control features:

- **[Public keys](/guides/public-keys)** — restrict a public key to devices with specific tags, so the key only authenticates against those devices.
- **[Firewall rules](/guides/firewall-rules)** — scope a rule to tagged devices, applying allow/deny policies to a group instead of individual hosts.

For example:

- Tag production servers with `production`, staging with `staging`
- Create a deploy key filtered to `production` — it only works on production devices
- Create a dev key filtered to `staging` — it only works on staging devices

This gives you environment-level access control without managing individual device permissions.

## Common patterns

| Tags | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `production`, `staging`, `dev` | Environment separation |
| `us-east`, `eu-west` | Geographic location |
| `web`, `database`, `worker` | Server role |

## Editing tags

Tags can be added or removed at any time without affecting device connectivity. Removing a tag immediately updates any public key or firewall rule filters that reference it.

---

# Team

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/team.mdx

title: Team
description: Manage namespace members, roles, and API keys

# Team

The Team page is where you manage who has access to your namespace and what they can do. It has two sections: **Members** and **API Keys**.

## Members

Members are users who have access to the current namespace. Each member has a role that determines their permissions.

![The Team page showing the Members tab with members and their roles](/img/team/members.png)

### Adding a member

1. Go to **Team** in the sidebar
2. Click **Add Member**
3. Enter the user's email address (they need an existing ShellHub account)
4. Select a role
5. Click **Add Member**

An invitation is sent to that email, and the user gains access once they accept it.

### Roles

| Role | Devices | Sessions | Keys & Rules | Members | Settings |
|------|---------|----------|--------------|---------|----------|
| **Owner** | Full | Full | Full | Full | Full |
| **Administrator** | Full | Full | Full | Add/Remove | Edit |
| **Operator** | Connect | View | View | — | — |
| **Observer** | View only | View | View | — | — |

**Owner** — Full control over the namespace, including deleting it. Each namespace has exactly one owner. Ownership cannot be transferred through the UI.

**Administrator** — Can manage devices, keys, firewall rules, and members. Cannot delete the namespace or change the owner.

**Operator** — Can connect to devices and view resources. Cannot create, edit, or delete anything.

**Observer** — Read-only access. Can view devices, sessions, and keys but cannot connect or modify anything.

### Editing a member's role

Hover over a member row and click the edit icon. Select the new role and save. Role changes take effect immediately.

### Removing a member

Hover over a member row and click the delete icon. The member loses access to the namespace immediately. This does not delete their ShellHub account — they can still access other namespaces they belong to.

> You cannot edit or remove the namespace owner, and you cannot edit or remove yourself.

## API Keys

API keys let you authenticate with the ShellHub REST API without using your personal credentials. Use them for CI/CD pipelines, automation scripts, Terraform, Ansible, and other integrations. See the [API reference](/developers/api-reference) for the full list of endpoints.

### Generating a key

1. Switch to the **API Keys** tab
2. Click **Generate Key**
3. Enter a name (e.g. `ci-pipeline`, `terraform-prod`)
4. Select a role — the key inherits the same permissions as that role
5. Set an expiration (30 days, 60 days, 90 days, 1 year, or never)
6. Click **Generate Key**

> Copy the key immediately. You won't be able to see it again after closing the drawer.

### Using a key

Pass the API key in the `X-API-Key` header:

```bash
$ curl -H "X-API-Key: <your-api-key>" \
  https://shellhub.example.com/api/devices
```

Or with the ShellHub CLI and integrations that accept an API key.

### Key roles

API keys follow the same role permissions as members:

- **Administrator** — Full API access (create, update, delete resources)
- **Operator** — Read access plus connect
- **Observer** — Read-only API access

Choose the least privilege needed for your use case. A CI pipeline that only reads device status needs Observer, not Administrator.

### Expiration

Expired keys stop working immediately. The Team page shows an **Expired** badge on keys past their expiration date.

Set shorter expirations for keys used in less trusted environments. Use "Never" only for long-lived infrastructure automation where rotating keys is impractical.

### Editing and deleting keys

You can rename a key or change its role at any time. Deleting a key revokes it immediately — any integration using it will get authentication errors.

---

# Web Endpoints

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/guides/web-endpoints.mdx

title: Web Endpoints
description: Expose HTTP services running on remote devices through ShellHub web endpoints

import EditionBanner from '../../components/EditionBanner.astro';

# Web Endpoints

Access HTTP services running on your devices through ShellHub — without opening ports or configuring firewalls. A web endpoint is a unique public URL that tunnels HTTP traffic to a service running on one of your [devices](/guides/devices), reachable by host IP and port. Requests flow through the agent's existing connection, so you don't open ports or configure firewalls.

<EditionBanner />

The **Web Endpoints** page lists every endpoint in your namespace. Each row shows the generated public URL, the local target it forwards to (e.g. `127.0.0.1:5432`), the time remaining before it expires, and a delete action.

![The Web Endpoints page listing active endpoints with their public URLs, targets, and time remaining](/img/web-endpoints/web-endpoints.png)

## How it works

1. A device runs an HTTP service reachable at a host and port (e.g., `127.0.0.1:8080`)
2. You create a web endpoint in ShellHub pointing to that target
3. ShellHub generates a public URL that routes requests through the gateway to the device

No additional ports are opened on the device. Traffic flows through the same outbound WebSocket connection the agent already maintains.

The target host can be the device itself or any machine reachable on the device's network — the agent forwards the request from where it runs.

## Creating a web endpoint

From the **Web Endpoints** page in the ShellHub dashboard:

1. Click **New Endpoint**
2. Choose the [device](/guides/devices) that will forward the traffic
3. Enter the **host** and **port** of the service (e.g., `127.0.0.1` and `8080`)
4. Set a **TTL** (lifetime) for the endpoint — choose a fixed duration, or leave it unlimited to keep the endpoint until you delete it
5. Click **Create**

ShellHub generates a unique URL like:

```
https://abcdef1234.tunnel.cloud.shellhub.io
```

Open this URL in your browser to access the service running on the device.

## Use cases

- **Web dashboards** — Access Grafana, Prometheus, Node-RED, or any monitoring tool running on edge devices
- **Admin panels** — Reach device configuration interfaces without VPN or port forwarding
- **API endpoints** — Expose REST APIs running on devices for testing or integration
- **Development** — Preview web applications running on remote machines

## Limitations

- HTTP traffic only — web endpoints proxy HTTP/HTTPS, not arbitrary TCP
- The device must be online and connected to ShellHub
- Endpoints expire according to their TTL. The remaining time is shown on the Web Endpoints page, and an endpoint with a fixed lifetime has its timer reset each time its URL is accessed. After expiration the endpoint becomes inaccessible until you recreate it
- Recreating an endpoint with the same host and port reuses the previous URL
- Each endpoint maps to a single host and port

## Security

- Endpoint URLs are randomly generated and not guessable
- Access control follows your ShellHub namespace permissions
- Traffic between the client and ShellHub gateway is encrypted (HTTPS)
- Traffic between the gateway and the device flows through the agent's encrypted WebSocket tunnel

## Next steps

- [Connecting](/guides/connecting) — SSH access methods (web terminal, SSH client, GUI tools)
- [Features](/getting-started/features) — Overview of all ShellHub features
- [Editions](/getting-started/editions) — Compare Cloud and Enterprise capabilities

---

# Ansible

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/integration/ansible.mdx

title: Ansible
description: Use Ansible to manage ShellHub devices — inventory, playbooks, and SSH configuration

# Ansible

Manage your ShellHub-connected devices with Ansible. Since ShellHub provides standard SSH access through its gateway, Ansible works without any special modules or plugins.

## Inventory

Create an Ansible inventory using the ShellHub SSHID format. The `ansible_user` is the SSHID `username@namespace.device`, and `ansible_host` is the ShellHub gateway:

```ini
[webservers]
web-01 ansible_host=cloud.shellhub.io ansible_user=root@my-namespace.web-01
web-02 ansible_host=cloud.shellhub.io ansible_user=root@my-namespace.web-02

[edge-devices]
sensor-gw ansible_host=cloud.shellhub.io ansible_user=admin@my-namespace.sensor-gateway
camera-01 ansible_host=cloud.shellhub.io ansible_user=admin@my-namespace.camera-node-01
```

> **Note:** For self-hosted instances, replace `cloud.shellhub.io` with your server address.

## Authentication

Use public key authentication to avoid password prompts:

1. Upload your SSH public key in the ShellHub dashboard under **Public Keys**
2. Point Ansible to the private key:

```ini
[all:vars]
ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/.ssh/id_ed25519
```

Or pass it on the command line:

```bash
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini --private-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 playbook.yml
```

> **Note:** On the first connection Ansible verifies the gateway's SSH host key. For unattended runs, either add it up front with `ssh-keyscan cloud.shellhub.io >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts`, or set `host_key_checking = False` in `ansible.cfg`. Otherwise the run fails with `Host key verification failed`.

## Running playbooks

Run playbooks as you normally would:

```bash
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini deploy.yml
```

```bash
$ ansible -i inventory.ini edge-devices -m ping
```

Ansible connects through the ShellHub gateway transparently. No changes to your playbooks are needed — only the inventory and SSH config.

## Dynamic inventory

For larger fleets, don't maintain a static file. The [`shellhub.core`](https://github.com/shellhub-io/ansible-collection) collection ships an inventory plugin that pulls accepted devices straight from your namespace and turns ShellHub tags into Ansible groups:

```bash
$ ansible-galaxy collection install shellhub.core
```

Create an inventory source file whose name ends in `shellhub.yml`:

```yaml
# inventory.shellhub.yml
plugin: shellhub.core.devices
api_url: https://cloud.shellhub.io   # your server, for self-hosted
ssh_user: root
ssh_key: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
keyed_groups:
  - key: shellhub_tags               # each ShellHub tag becomes a group: tag_<name>
    prefix: tag
```

Provide a namespace API key and run:

```bash
$ export SHELLHUB_API_KEY=...
$ ansible-inventory -i inventory.shellhub.yml --graph
$ ansible -i inventory.shellhub.yml tag_production -m ping
```

Your ShellHub tags become Ansible groups automatically (`tag_production`, `tag_region_us`, …), so the inventory tracks the dashboard with no manual updates. The plugin paginates the device list and resolves the namespace from the API key.

## Next steps

- [Public Keys](/guides/public-keys) — Set up key-based authentication
- [Tags](/guides/tags) — Organize devices into groups for targeted automation
- [shellhub.core collection](https://github.com/shellhub-io/ansible-collection) — The dynamic inventory plugin

---

# CI/CD Pipelines

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/integration/ci-cd.mdx

title: CI/CD Pipelines
description: Deploy to ShellHub devices and debug CI runners from GitHub Actions and other CI/CD pipelines

# CI/CD Pipelines

From your pipeline you can reach your devices over SSH two ways: deploy code and run commands on them, or drop into the CI runner itself to debug a failing build. Both go through the ShellHub gateway, addressed by SSHID (`user@namespace.device@gateway`), so the target needs no public IP and no inbound ports — the gateway routes the session through the agent's reverse tunnel.

## Deploy to a device (GitHub Actions)

Use [`appleboy/ssh-action`](https://github.com/appleboy/ssh-action) to run commands on a device. You need an online device and an SSH key registered in ShellHub — store its private key as a secret (recommended over a password). Address the device by its SSHID: `host` is the gateway, `username` is `<user>@<namespace>.<device>`.

```yaml
name: Deploy to device
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: cloud.shellhub.io
          port: 22
          username: deploy@my-namespace.web-server
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /app && git pull && systemctl restart myapp
```

The agent has no public IP and no inbound ports — ShellHub routes the session through the reverse tunnel. Copying files works the same way with [`appleboy/scp-action`](https://github.com/appleboy/scp-action).

## Debug a CI runner (GitHub Actions)

To SSH into a live runner and debug a failing build, use the [`shellhub-io/ci-action`](https://github.com/shellhub-io/ci-action). It needs a namespace API key with device accept/remove permission, stored as a secret. The action registers the runner as an ephemeral device, authorizes your keys, prints an `ssh` command and a web-terminal URL, and removes the device when the job ends:

```yaml
      - name: Open a ShellHub debug session on this runner
        uses: shellhub-io/ci-action@v1
        with:
          server: https://cloud.shellhub.io
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.SHELLHUB_TENANT_ID }}
          api-key: ${{ secrets.SHELLHUB_API_KEY }}
          authorize-actor: auto   # authorize the GitHub keys of whoever triggered the run
```

No public session URL is ever printed — the runner shows up in your namespace and you reach it by SSHID from your own machine, governed by namespace RBAC and recorded. The job blocks until you connect and disconnect; run `sudo touch /continue` to release it early. See [`ci-action-demo`](https://github.com/shellhub-io/ci-action-demo) for a complete, runnable workflow.

## Other CI/CD systems

Any system that can run SSH commands works with ShellHub. The pattern is always the same:

1. Install an SSH client in the build environment
2. Write the private key from a secret/variable to `~/.ssh/`
3. Connect using the ShellHub SSHID format: `user@namespace.device@gateway`

This works with Jenkins, CircleCI, Drone, Bitbucket Pipelines, Azure DevOps, and any other CI/CD tool.

## Best practices

- **Use dedicated keys** — Create an SSH key pair specifically for CI/CD. Don't reuse personal keys.
- **Scope keys narrowly** — In ShellHub, scope the public key to only the devices and usernames your pipeline needs.
- **Use device tags** — Tag devices by environment (`production`, `staging`) and scope keys to tags rather than individual devices.

---

# Integrations

Source: https://github.com/shellhub-io/shellhub/blob/master/ui/apps/docs/src/pages/integration/overview.mdx

title: Integrations
description: Integrate ShellHub with Ansible, Terraform, CI/CD, VS Code, and HTTP tunnels

# Integrations

ShellHub works with the tools you already use. Because every device is reachable through a standard SSH connection via the ShellHub gateway, anything that speaks SSH can connect to your devices — no special plugins or proprietary protocols required.

## What you can integrate

| Integration | What it does |
|---|---|
| [Ansible](/integration/ansible) | Automate configuration management and deployments across your fleet |
| [Terraform](/integration/terraform) | Provision infrastructure with the agent pre-installed |
| [CI/CD Pipelines](/integration/ci-cd) | Deploy, test, or provision devices from GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and other pipelines |
| [VS Code Remote SSH](/integration/vscode-remote) | Develop directly on remote devices from VS Code |

## How integrations work

All SSH-based integrations follow the same pattern:

1. Connect to the ShellHub gateway (e.g., `cloud.shellhub.io`) on port 22
2. Use the device's SSHID as the target: `username@namespace.device`
3. Authenticate with password or public key

The gateway routes the connection to the correct device through the agent's reverse tunnel. From the client's perspective, it behaves like a normal SSH connection.

```bash
$ ssh user@namespace.device@cloud.shellhub.io
```

## Public key authentication

For automation workflows (Ansible, CI/CD), public key authentication avoids storing passwords in scripts or environment variables:

1. Upload your public key in the ShellHub dashboard under **Public Keys**
2. Scope the key to specific usernames, hostnames, or device tags
3. Use the corresponding private key in your automation tool

See [Public Keys](/guides/public-keys) for setup details.

## Next steps

- [Ansible](/integration/ansible) — Automate device management
- [Terraform](/integration/terraform) — Provision infra with the agent pre-installed
- [CI/CD Pipelines](/integration/ci-cd) — Integrate with your deployment pipeline
- [VS Code Remote SSH](/integration/vscode-remote) — Remote development on devices
